title: Lincoln Park Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Lincoln Park wells have a 50-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock can make drilling cost $9,200-$17,000.
h1: What Lincoln Park Well Records Tell Buyers
intro_html:
Lincoln Park sits in a mountain setting where well conditions can change quickly from one property to the next. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records include 1,256 permitted wells, with 864 recorded as constructed. The records point to generally shallow wells, but fractured mountain bedrock still makes a new drilling project site-specific.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Use these figures to set expectations, not to guarantee water on a particular lot. A neighboring well, its construction report, and the current permit requirements deserve review before you buy or build.

sections.heading: Lincoln Park Well Depth Depends on the Bedrock
sections.html:
The recorded median well depth near Lincoln Park is 50 feet. The middle half runs from 34 to 89 feet, and 77% of reported wells are under 100 feet. That is useful for early budgeting: a typical bid may be based on a relatively shallow hole, not automatically on a several-hundred-foot well.

The spread is still important. About 13% of wells are 100 to 300 feet, 6% are 300 to 600 feet, and 4% exceed 600 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 293 feet, while the deepest record reaches 2,200 feet. Granite and gneiss can fracture differently across short distances, so a nearby shallow well does not guarantee the same result on your parcel.

sections.heading: Expected Well Yield Around Lincoln Park
sections.html:
Among the 181 records that report pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half falls between 4.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. That is a workable range for many household uses, but a yield report is not the same as a guarantee of continuous supply or storage capacity.

About 3% of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, 25% produce 1 to 5, 43% produce 5 to 15, and 30% produce more than 15. For a buyer, the low-yield group is the warning: confirm the well's test, pressure tank, storage, and recovery information. If a property will need irrigation or several residences, verify the permit and water-right requirements rather than relying on the median.

sections.heading: Water Levels and the Local Record
sections.html:
Only 25 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. In those records, the median depth to water is 44 feet, with the middle half between 16 and 100 feet. That gives a starting point for pump and trench planning, but it does not establish the water level beneath every Lincoln Park lot.

The permit counts by decade do not show a continuous water-level trend because the available facts do not provide water-level measurements by decade. They do show the largest permit period in the 1990s, with 379 permits, followed by 215 in the 2000s. Treat the static-water figures as property-specific evidence to verify, not proof that the regional table is rising or falling.

sections.heading: Who Has Drilled Near Lincoln Park
sections.html:
Permit records extend from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. The most active named records belong to Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 438, followed by Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.) with 71 and Young'S Drilling & Pump Serv (Young, Nolen) with 63. These are record counts, not a guarantee of current availability, price, or workmanship.

Household and domestic permits make up 45% of the use mix. Stock accounts for 13%, irrigation 3%, and monitoring 42%. That large monitoring share matters when comparing records: not every mapped well is a home-water source. Ask the driller to review construction reports and confirm the intended use before using a nearby permit as a direct comparison.

sections.heading: What a Lincoln Park Well May Cost
sections.html:
Drilling here means working in fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $3,200 to $5,000. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,200 to $17,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole can move the total higher, and difficult access or an uncertain fracture can affect the bid. Request a written estimate that states the assumed depth, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, electrical work, trenching, and what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than expected.

sections.heading: Lincoln Park Risks to Check Before Building
sections.html:
Water quality deserves a separate review from well yield. Within about 10 miles, the records map 32 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 94 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove contamination at a particular property, but they are reasons to check site history and order a qualified water test before closing.

Low yield and dry-hole risk also remain possible in fractured bedrock, even with a 10.0-gallon-per-minute median. Confirm the well location, construction report, pumping test, static level, casing, and grout. Before placing a septic system or house, verify setbacks, access for a rig, soil and percolation conditions, electrical routing, and the permit requirements for the intended household use. An augmentation plan may matter in an over-appropriated basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Lincoln Park, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth near Lincoln Park is 50 feet, and the middle half of wells is 34 to 89 feet. About 77% are under 100 feet. Conditions vary widely in fractured granite and gneiss: 4% of records exceed 600 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 2,200 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Lincoln Park?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $3,200 to $5,000. A finished system including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,200 to $17,000. A deeper or difficult hole can require a larger budget.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Lincoln Park?
faq.a: Among 181 records reporting yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 4.0 to 15.0. About 3% produce under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the specific well's pumping test and recovery information, because fractured-bedrock results can differ substantially between nearby properties.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Lincoln Park, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from the well map alone. Within about 10 miles are 32 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 94 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those facts call for a property-specific laboratory test and a review of local site history before using the water for a household.

faq.q: Are there many household wells near Lincoln Park?
faq.a: Yes. Domestic and household uses account for 45% of the permit records within 5 miles, although monitoring wells account for 42%. The full record contains 1,256 permitted wells, with 864 recorded as constructed. Confirm that a nearby well is actually a household source and compare its permit, depth, yield, and construction report.
